speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I see you have blisters on your forearm and ulcers on your mucosal surfaces. To help narrow this down, can you tell me if you have experienced any fever, fatigue, or recent sun exposure? Also, have you noticed any rash on your hands or feet?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old female. The patient reports the appearance of blisters on her forearm 3 days ago, accompanied by pain in her left cheek when eating and pain during sexual intercourse for the past week. She has been hiking in the woods recently but denies contact with poison ivy. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis, recently started taking captopril, and discontinued meloxicam 2 weeks ago. Family history includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That history of drug initiation is very important; did the blisters and oral pain start shortly after you began taking the captopril? Also, please describe if these blisters appear on your palms or soles of your feet.

REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count with Differential, Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, and C3/C4 Complement levels.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT WITH DIFFERENTIAL: WITHIN NORMAL LIMITS; COMPREHENSIVE METABOLIC PANEL: WITHIN NORMAL LIMITS; C3/C4 COMPLEMENT LEVELS: WITHIN NORMAL LIMITS

speaker: Patient
text: includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Cellulitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: Direct Immunofluorescence and Tissue Biopsy of the forearm lesion. REQUEST IMAGES: Dermatology photos of the forearm blisters and oral ulcers. Did you notice your fingernails have become detached or develop ridges since starting the captopril?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Direct Immunofluorescence: Intercellular IgG and C3 deposition within the epidermis; Tissue Biopsy: Acantholysis and intraepidermal blister formation; Dermatology Photos: Multiple flaccid blisters on the volar surface of the forearm with mucosal ulcers present on buccal, gingival, and vulvar surfaces; Fingernails: No detachment or ridging observed.

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on the biopsy showing acantholysis and immunofluorescence with intercellular IgG, along with your mucosal involvement, this is not cellulitis but rather Pemphigus Vulgaris. The captopril may have acted as a trigger, but the underlying autoimmune process is distinct. Given your recent hiking in the woods, I need to rule out other causes; did you experience any new joint swelling or morning stiffness beyond your known osteoarthritis?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Hypertension, osteoarthritis. Social history: Has started hiking in the woods on weekends. No relevant travel history.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Pemphigus Vulgaris. The combination of flaccid blisters on the skin, painful oral and genital ulcers, acantholysis on biopsy, and intercellular IgG deposits confirms this autoimmune blistering disease, likely triggered by the recent initiation of captopril. We will proceed with high-dose systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants to halt disease progression.
